Design choices

Source: vignettes/articles/design.Rmd
design.Rmd
library(anovakit)

Every anovakit function follows the same rules about what it prints, which settings can change a result, and what it decides for you. Each is shown below on a small example; for the object itself see Working with results.

Nothing prints

No analysis function writes to the console, and no plot is drawn as a side effect. Warnings and messages raised while fitting by car, emmeans, sandwich, afex and base R’s model functions are captured and recorded in $notes instead of reaching the console. Here a logistic regression with separation in one group prints nothing, and the second of its notes describes the problem:

sep <- data.frame(
  group = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), each = 10),
  y     = c(rep(0, 10), rep(c(0, 1), 5), rep(c(0, 1, 1, 1, 1), 2))
)
out <- capture.output(fit_sep <- anova_bin(sep, "y", "group", plots = FALSE))
length(out)
#> [1] 0
writeLines(strwrap(fit_sep$notes[2], 72))
#> Complete or quasi-complete separation detected: the fitted probability
#> is numerically 0 or 1 in group = a. The affected coefficient(s):
#> groupb, groupc. An affected odds ratio is not identified: it will be
#> enormous, its interval will be unbounded on one side, and its Wald
#> p-value will be near 1 no matter how strong the association is; the
#> same goes for that cell's marginal probability and the comparisons
#> involving it. With events this sparse the likelihood-ratio omnibus test
#> is also liberal. Consider a penalised fit such as logistf::logistf(),
#> or collapsing the offending level.

verbose = TRUE reports progress through message(), so suppressMessages() silences it. Plots are built and stored in $plots; they appear only when you print one.

conf_level sets every interval

One argument sets the level of every interval in the tables a function returns: group and marginal means, pairwise differences, effect sizes, odds and rate ratios, simple slopes and the error bars in the plots.

fit90 <- anova_glm(chickwts, "weight", "feed", conf_level = 0.90,
                   plots = FALSE)
fit90$conf_level
#> [1] 0.9
head(fit90$posthoc[, c("contrast", "estimate", "conf_low", "conf_high")], 3)
#>             contrast  estimate  conf_low conf_high
#> 1 casein - horsebean 163.38333 101.15257  225.6141
#> 2   casein - linseed 104.83333  45.49863  164.1680
#> 3  casein - meatmeal  46.67424 -13.99399  107.3425

It does not reach $emmeans_object. That is emmeans’ own reference grid, and it carries emmeans’ default level of 0.95. Pass the level to the function that summarises the grid, such as confint(); given to contrast() it has no effect on the intervals:

ctl <- emmeans::contrast(fit90$emmeans_object, "trt.vs.ctrl")
confint(ctl, level = fit90$conf_level)
#>  contrast           estimate   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
#>  horsebean - casein  -163.38 23.5 65   -217.3  -109.47
#>  linseed - casein    -104.83 22.4 65   -156.2   -53.43
#>  meatmeal - casein    -46.67 22.9 65    -99.2     5.88
#>  soybean - casein     -77.15 21.6 65   -126.7   -27.62
#>  sunflower - casein     5.33 22.4 65    -46.1    56.74
#> 
#> Degrees-of-freedom method: user-specified 
#> Confidence level used: 0.9 
#> Conf-level adjustment: dunnettx method for 5 estimates

Type II by default, and what Type III means

anova_manova(), anova_bin(), anova_count() and anova_glm() report Type II tests by default. Each main effect is tested after the other main effects, and the result does not depend on how the factors are coded. anova_ancova() and anova_rm() default to Type III; the ANCOVA and repeated measures walkthroughs explain their tables. The type used is printed in the heading and stored in attr(fit$anova, "ss_type").

When you ask for type = "III", the model is fitted under sum-to-zero contrasts. In a model with an interaction, a Type III main-effect row tests the main effect only under those contrasts. Under R’s default treatment contrasts, car::Anova(type = 3) tests the simple effect of each factor at the reference level of the other, and still labels the table Type III.

The warpbreaks data with the first five rows removed make an unbalanced two-way design:

wb <- warpbreaks[-(1:5), ]
t3 <- anova_glm(wb, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"), interaction = TRUE,
                type = "III", plots = FALSE)
unlist(t3$model$contrasts)
#>        wool     tension 
#> "contr.sum" "contr.sum"
t3$anova
#>           term   sum_sq df statistic      p_value
#> 1         wool  588.751  1  6.343522 0.0155817964
#> 2      tension 2002.165  2 10.786206 0.0001597943
#> 3 wool:tension 1121.446  2  6.041534 0.0048717187
#> 4    Residuals 3990.889 43        NA           NA

The same model fitted with treatment contrasts and passed to car gives a different wool row, which is the effect of wool at tension = "L" only:

car::Anova(lm(breaks ~ wool * tension, data = wb), type = 3)["wool", ]
#> Anova Table (Type III tests)
#> 
#> Response: breaks
#>      Sum Sq Df F value    Pr(>F)    
#> wool 1195.5  1  12.881 0.0008449 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

A model with aliased coefficients, such as one with an empty cell, has no Type III tests. The function then computes Type II tests, and the heading, $method and $notes say so.

Covariates are centred

anova_ancova() mean-centres every covariate before fitting (center_covariates = TRUE), and anova_manova() centres its covariates too. Centring always moves the intercept to the covariate mean. When the model contains a group-by-covariate term and type = "III", it also moves the group row, because that row then tests the groups at covariate = 0. On a baseline score distributed around 100, zero is far from the data:

set.seed(2024)
n <- 240
trial <- data.frame(
  arm      = factor(rep(c("placebo", "low", "high"), each = n / 3)),
  baseline = rnorm(n, mean = 100, sd = 12)
)
effect <- c(placebo = 0, low = 3, high = 7)[as.character(trial$arm)]
trial$score <- 0.6 * trial$baseline + effect + rnorm(n, 0, 6)

centred <- anova_ancova(trial, "score", "arm", "baseline",
                        force_interaction = TRUE, plots = FALSE)
uncentred <- anova_ancova(trial, "score", "arm", "baseline",
                          force_interaction = TRUE,
                          center_covariates = FALSE, plots = FALSE)
data.frame(term        = centred$anova$term,
           p_centred   = signif(centred$anova$p_value, 3),
           p_uncentred = signif(uncentred$anova$p_value, 3))
#>           term p_centred p_uncentred
#> 1     baseline  3.80e-52    3.80e-52
#> 2          arm  6.53e-11    9.96e-01
#> 3 baseline:arm  6.91e-01    6.91e-01
#> 4    Residuals        NA          NA
all.equal(centred$emmeans, uncentred$emmeans)
#> [1] TRUE

On the same rows, the arm row has p = 6.5e-11 centred and p = 0.996 uncentred. The other rows and the marginal means are the same, because $emmeans, $posthoc and $simple_slopes are always evaluated with every covariate at its mean (a 0/1 covariate included). In the additive model, and under Type II, centring does not change the group row. The means subtracted are in $covariate_means.

The ANCOVA model is chosen by a test unless you fix it

By default anova_ancova() chooses between the additive and the separate-slopes model with a homogeneity-of-slopes test on the same data, and records the choice in $notes. The p-values that follow do not allow for that selection. If the test misses a real slope difference, the group row and $posthoc reject more often than their nominal level: somewhat so when the groups were randomised, and far more so when the groups’ covariate means differ, which $notes points out. force_interaction = TRUE fixes the separate-slopes model in advance and avoids the selection step. With several grouping factors, anova_ancova() fits their interaction by default (interaction = TRUE), as a factorial ANCOVA does. The ANCOVA walkthrough covers both choices in detail.

Comparisons follow the model

When grouping factors enter a model additively (interaction = FALSE, the default except in anova_ancova()), $emmeans and $posthoc are reported for each factor on its own, averaged over the others, with a term column and one multiplicity family per factor. Comparing every cell would repeat each main-effect difference once per level of the other factors, and adjust for comparisons that carry no extra information.

additive <- anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                      plots = FALSE)
additive$emmeans[, c("term", "wool", "tension", "estimate")]
#>      term wool tension estimate
#> 1    wool    A    <NA> 31.03704
#> 2    wool    B    <NA> 25.25926
#> 3 tension <NA>       L 36.38889
#> 4 tension <NA>       M 26.38889
#> 5 tension <NA>       H 21.66667
additive$posthoc[, c("term", "contrast", "p_adjusted")]
#>      term contrast  p_adjusted
#> 1    wool    A - B 0.073613669
#> 2 tension    L - M 0.033626219
#> 3 tension    L - H 0.001121788
#> 4 tension    M - H 0.447421021

When the model contains the interaction, the cells are compared:

cells <- anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                   interaction = TRUE, plots = FALSE)
nrow(cells$emmeans)
#> [1] 6
nrow(cells$posthoc)
#> [1] 15

A level combination with no data is left out when the model cannot estimate it, and named in $notes when the model estimates it by extrapolation (as an additive model does). With no model to follow, anova_welch() and anova_kw() combine the grouping columns into one factor of the cells that contain data and compare those.

Every argument is named

No modelling function has a ... argument except anova_rm(), and that one accepts only fun_aggregate, observed, type and anova_table = list(p_adjust_method = ), passed to afex::aov_ez(). Anything else is refused by name rather than ignored:

rm_data <- data.frame(id = rep(1:6, each = 2), time = rep(c("pre", "post"), 6),
                      y = c(5, 7, 4, 6, 6, 9, 5, 5, 7, 8, 4, 7))
try(anova_rm(rm_data, "y", "id", "time", es = "pes"))
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'lme4':
#>   method           from
#>   na.action.merMod car
#> Error : anova_rm() has no argument `es`, so it would be ignored. The arguments passed on to afex::aov_ez() through `...` may only be: fun_aggregate, observed, type, anova_table.

Every argument that reaches a fitting call is named, so nothing can be passed through that overrides a decision the function has made. A contrasts = argument, for example, would defeat type = "III" while the table still said Type III, so it is an unused argument:

try(anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", "tension", contrasts = list()))
#> Error in anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", "tension", contrasts = list()) : 
#>   unused argument (contrasts = list())

A column may play only one role (response, group, covariate, weights, offset or subject):

try(anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", "tension", weights = "breaks"))
#> Error : Column `breaks` is given as both the response and the weights; a column can play only one role.

Weights are named as a column too, so they stay aligned with the rows; Weights and robust standard errors explains what happens to zero weights.

Global settings do not change results

Options set for some other analysis in the same session do not change a fit’s results. afex::afex_options() cannot change an anova_rm() fit, because the type, the contrasts and the emmeans model are all set explicitly. The emmeans::emm_options() settings that change a result (adjustment, sidedness, null, degrees of freedom, scale) are cleared for the duration of the fit; only computational limits such as rg.limit are kept, so you can still let a large grid through. Here an emm_options() setting that turns off every adjustment leaves the Tukey adjustment in place:

emmeans::emm_options(contrast = list(adjust = "none"))
tension <- anova_glm(warpbreaks, "breaks", "tension", plots = FALSE)
tension$posthoc[, c("contrast", "p_value", "p_adjusted", "adjustment")]
#>   contrast      p_value  p_adjusted adjustment
#> 1    L - M 0.0147169627 0.038459768      tukey
#> 2    L - H 0.0005008605 0.001431503      tukey
#> 3    M - H 0.2386143753 0.463083097      tukey
emmeans::emm_options(contrast = NULL)

The global contrasts option can change how a Type II model’s coefficients are coded, but not its tests, marginal means or comparisons; type = "III" always fits under sum-to-zero contrasts, and odds and rate ratios always come from a treatment-coded fit.

The only option of its own that anovakit reads is anovakit.theme, which sets the base theme of every plot and changes no result; the plots guide shows how to use it.

Assumption checks match the method

Each function checks the assumptions its own method makes. anova_welch() tests normality within each group rather than on pooled residuals. Pooling groups with different variances produces a mixture that can fail a normality test when every group is normal, which would argue against the method being used. For the same reason anova_rm() tests the within-subject residuals in each within-subject cell.

welch <- anova_welch(chickwts, "weight", "feed", plots = FALSE)
welch$assumptions$normality[, c("group", "n", "statistic", "p_value")]
#>       group  n statistic   p_value
#> 1    casein 12 0.9166257 0.2591841
#> 2 horsebean 10 0.9375834 0.5264499
#> 3   linseed 12 0.9693128 0.9034734
#> 4  meatmeal 11 0.9791381 0.9611795
#> 5   soybean 14 0.9464029 0.5063768
#> 6 sunflower 12 0.9280884 0.3602904

anova_kw() assumes no distribution, so it runs no checks unless you ask with diagnostics = TRUE:

length(anova_kw(chickwts, "weight", "feed", plots = FALSE)$assumptions)
#> [1] 0
names(anova_kw(chickwts, "weight", "feed", plots = FALSE,
               diagnostics = TRUE)$assumptions)
#> [1] "normality"

The diagnostics guide lists every check by function and what to do when one fails.

Robust standard errors

vcov_type = "HC0" to "HC4" on anova_ancova(), anova_bin(), anova_count() and anova_glm() changes the standard errors in the coefficient table and in the marginal means and comparisons. In anova_ancova() it also reaches the F tests (as robust Wald F tests) and the simple slopes, and in the other three the omnibus table when test_statistic = "Wald". Likelihood-ratio tests rest on the model. Where fitted values sit on the boundary (separation, an all-zero group) or a cell has one observation, the model-based covariance is used, with a note. Weights and robust standard errors gives the rules, including how whole-number weights are treated as frequency weights.

Multiplicity adjustments depend on the method

anova_welch() and anova_kw() compare groups directly and accept the p.adjust() methods, defaulting to "holm" and "BH". The other six take their comparisons from emmeans, which also offers "tukey" (their default), "sidak", "scheffe" and "dunnettx". Every $posthoc table reports the unadjusted p-value in p_value, the adjusted one in p_adjusted and the method in adjustment, as the table above shows.

The intervals in $posthoc from the emmeans-based functions are simultaneous. emmeans cannot turn a step-down method such as Holm’s into intervals and uses Bonferroni intervals instead; $notes says when that happens. anova_welch() reports a per-comparison interval for each pair.

Notes record every decision

Whenever a function chooses something on your behalf, it says so in $notes: the model chosen by a slopes test or a dispersion statistic, a centred covariate, dropped rows or subjects, a fallback from Type III to Type II, an odds ratio that is not identified. The ANCOVA above, fitted without force_interaction, records two decisions:

writeLines(anova_ancova(trial, "score", "arm", "baseline", plots = FALSE)$notes)
#> Covariate(s) mean-centred before fitting (baseline: 100.3), so the intercept refers to the covariate mean rather than to covariate = 0. $emmeans are evaluated at the covariate mean either way.
#> Slopes are consistent with being equal across groups (p = 0.6908), so the additive model was used. A non-significant test is not proof of equal slopes, only an absence of evidence against it, and the p-values below do not allow for the model having been chosen by a test on these same data: if the slopes do differ, the group row and $posthoc can reject more often than their nominal level, somewhat so even when the groups were randomised and far more so when the groups' covariate means are unequal. Setting force_interaction = TRUE in advance avoids the selection step.

Missing optional packages are recorded the same way. Without MASS, anova_count(model = "auto") fits a quasi-Poisson model where it would have chosen a negative binomial, and without sandwich a vcov_type request falls back to model-based standard errors; each records the fallback in $notes. anova_rm() without afex, and anova_count(model = "negbin") without MASS, stop with an error instead.

Working with results shows how to read and search the notes, and how $data_used and $n_removed account for every row you supplied.
